title: What Actually Happens If You Fall Into a Black Hole?
creator: Priya Raman
description:
Spaghettification, frozen clocks and the edge you can never see yourself cross. Dev and I fall into a black hole (hypothetically).

Thanks to Keyward for sponsoring this episode. Get 3 months free at https://keyward.com/orbit

Further reading in the pinned comment.

sentences.t: Okay Dev, I need you to imagine you've been very bad and we're throwing you into a black hole.
Wow, great start, love that for me.
No, but seriously, what actually happens to you on the way in is one of the weirdest things in all of physics.
So let's pick a black hole first, because the size really matters here.
Let's start with a small one, about ten times the mass of the Sun, the kind you get when a big star collapses.
The event horizon on that is only about sixty kilometers across, so roughly the size of a city.
And the problem with a small black hole is the tides.
Gravity gets stronger the closer you are, so if you're falling in feet first, your feet are being pulled way harder than your head.
Physicists genuinely call this spaghettification, and I promise I did not make that up.
You get stretched into a long thin noodle of atoms well before you even reach the horizon.
Okay that's horrible, can we pick a nicer black hole?
We can, actually, and this is the counterintuitive part.
A supermassive black hole, like the one in the middle of our galaxy, is so huge that the tides at the horizon are actually gentle.
You could float across the event horizon and not feel anything at all.
Dev, quick question before we cross it, do you know who's sponsoring today's episode?
Is it the password people again?
It is the password people, it's Keyward.
Keyward is a password manager, so it creates a long random password for every account you have and remembers them all for you.
It fills them in on your laptop and your phone, and it warns you if any of your logins show up in a data breach.
Dev used to use the same password for everything, and I'm not going to say what it was, but it had his cat's name in it.
Rude, but accurate.
You can share logins safely with your family too, so nobody's texting the streaming password around anymore.
Go to keyward.com/orbit and you get three months free on any plan.
Okay, so you've drifted past the horizon of our nice big black hole.
From your point of view, nothing dramatic happens at that exact moment.
There's no wall, no flash, no sign saying welcome.
But now every possible path you could take, in every direction, leads further in.
The center isn't really a place in front of you anymore, it's more like a moment in your future.
That's so much creepier than spaghetti.
Right, and now here's the part I love, which is what I see, watching you from a safe distance.
Because of time dilation, as you get closer to the horizon, your clock looks slower and slower to me.
Your light also gets stretched redder and dimmer.
So from my side, I never actually see you cross.
You just slowly freeze and fade at the edge, like a photo that's fading out.
So for you I'm gone in a flash, and for me you're stuck there forever?
Basically, yes, although you fade so fast that in practice you'd vanish from view pretty quickly.
And eventually, even in the big black hole, the tides do win, deeper in, and the noodle situation happens anyway.
Great, so the nice black hole just delays the noodle.
Exactly, it's a scenic route to the noodle.
Next week we're doing the opposite question, which is what happens if you fall into a neutron star, and spoiler, it's worse.
Thanks for watching, everyone, see you next week.
